blog_posts.title: Building Across Backend, AI, and Connected Systems
blog_posts.content:
# Building Across Backend, AI, and Connected Systems

My work spans backend engineering, applied machine learning, computer vision, and embedded systems. The common thread is turning technical ideas into systems people can use.

## Building dependable software

At Telite Systems, I contribute to a multi-tenant Learning Management System. I work across FastAPI and PostgreSQL services, React interfaces, Docker-based environments, and GitHub Actions workflows. Working across those layers has taught me to follow a feature beyond the code: through integration, troubleshooting, and deployment.

## Exploring intelligent applications

My machine learning and computer vision projects include a Scikit-learn model served through Flask and a YOLOv8n/OpenCV obstacle detection robot. These projects have given me practical experience connecting model output to an application or physical system.

## Designing for unreliable environments

For a disaster-management mesh network, I explored ESP32 and LoRa communication, self-healing routing, encrypted telemetry, and a dashboard for network visibility. The project brought software, electronics, and resilience concerns together.

I am especially interested in backend and software engineering roles where I can keep learning, contribute across the stack, and build reliable products with a thoughtful team.

blog_posts.title: How I isolated tenant data with PostgreSQL row-level security
blog_posts.content:
# How I isolated tenant data with PostgreSQL row-level security

A multi-tenant learning platform has to keep each organization’s records inside its own boundary. At Telite Systems, I contributed to an LMS for company and college organizations, designed for 5,000–10,000 users. Tenant isolation was part of the data model and request path, not an afterthought.

## Keep the organization boundary explicit

The platform uses `org_id` to associate tenant-owned records with an organization. API authorization checks the user’s role and organization permissions. PostgreSQL row-level security adds a database-level boundary around access to those records.

These layers address different failure modes: application checks decide whether an operation is allowed, while row policies help prevent an accidentally broad query from exposing another organization’s rows.

## Apply the same thinking across features

The LMS included courses, progress, quizzes, enrolments, assignments, gradebook, notifications, and administration. A tenant boundary needs to stay consistent across every feature that reads or changes organization data. That made it important to consider the organization context alongside endpoint permissions and database access.

As part of a four-person team moving from a Moodle prototype to a custom platform, I developed FastAPI and PostgreSQL endpoints and responsive React components. The work reinforced a useful principle for me: tenant isolation is a property of the whole request path, from authorization to the final database query.

## What I learned

Row-level security is strongest when the application’s authorization model and database policies express the same tenant boundary. It provides defense in depth, while clear organization scoping keeps the design understandable to the team maintaining it.

blog_posts.title: Two-stage retrieval: Qdrant plus a FlashRank reranker, and what it changed
blog_posts.content:
# Two-stage retrieval: Qdrant plus a FlashRank reranker, and what it changed

For my Enterprise Agentic RAG project, I wanted retrieval to do more than pass the nearest vector matches straight to a language model. I built a two-stage pipeline: broad semantic search first, then a cross-encoder reranking pass to prioritize a smaller context set.

## Retrieve broadly, then rerank

The ingestion pipeline handles PDF, HTML, DOCX, PPTX, and TXT files. It creates chunks of about 1,500 characters and batches their embeddings. At query time, Gemini 3072-dimensional embeddings search Qdrant using cosine similarity. I retrieve the top 15 candidates, then use FlashRank to rerank them and pass the top 5 onward.

The retriever gives the system a candidate set with useful semantic recall. The reranker then scores each candidate against the query, helping order the context by query relevance before the responder uses it.

## What changed in the pipeline

The main change was the handoff: the responder receives a shorter, reranked context instead of the initial vector results as-is. I manually reviewed retrieval on an 83-chunk corpus that included distractor documents, which helped me inspect whether the ranking step placed useful passages ahead of plausible but less relevant matches.

I have not treated that small manual review as a formal accuracy benchmark. End-to-end latency averaged about 15 seconds across 10 queries with a 120B model, so that figure reflects the complete agent flow rather than retrieval alone.

## The broader system

The pipeline runs inside a LangGraph Planner–Retriever–Responder state machine with conversation memory, served through FastAPI and a Streamlit interface. Retry/backoff and Logfire tracing help make the flow easier to observe.

This project taught me to treat retrieval quality as a pipeline design problem: candidate generation, reranking, context size, evaluation, and latency all influence the final experience.

blog_posts.title: Designing a LoRa mesh that heals itself
blog_posts.content:
# Designing a LoRa mesh that heals itself

For my B.Tech major project, I worked on a decentralized, solar-powered mesh radio network for disaster management. The goal was to keep communication useful when an individual node failed, instead of making every device depend on one fixed path.

## Route around a failed node

The network uses ESP32 nodes communicating over LoRa. I implemented Dijkstra-based routing so nodes can find paths through the mesh and reroute when a node becomes unavailable. That self-healing behavior is central to the design: a broken path should trigger a new route rather than stop the whole network.

## Make the telemetry useful and protected

Nodes carry GPS and environmental telemetry, including temperature, rainfall, and soil moisture. AES-128 encryption protects that telemetry. A real-time web dashboard presents network status and SOS alerts so operators can see what the network is reporting.

## What the project brought together

This work combined embedded programming, routing, radio communication, data protection, and a user-facing dashboard. It also made reliability concrete: the system has to account for failures in the network itself, not only errors in application code.

The project was developed from February to June 2026 using ESP32 and LoRa. It strengthened my interest in building systems that remain useful when their operating environment is unpredictable.
